# Mathematical and physical toolbox {#sec-toolbox}

## Units and nondimensionalization

The basic walk has a time scale $\tau_0$ and a speed $v$. These define a length $\ell_0=v\tau_0$. Introduce $T=t/\tau_0$, $Y=x/\ell_0$, and a dimensionless density $p(Y,T)=\ell_0P(\ell_0Y,\tau_0T)$. Then $\int p\,dY=1$ and the cone becomes $|Y|\le T$. For Lomax durations the dimensionless density is $\gamma(1+T)^{-1-\gamma}$. Only the tail index remains as a free shape parameter.

This rescaling explains why numerical examples can set $v=\tau_0=1$ without loss of generality for this model. To restore physical units in an MSD, multiply the dimensionless result by $(v\tau_0)^2$ and replace $T$ by $t/\tau_0$. For example $\langle Y^2\rangle\propto T^{3-\gamma}$ becomes $\langle X^2\rangle\propto v^2\tau_0^{\gamma-1}t^{3-\gamma}$. A prefactor with a different power of $\tau_0$ would fail dimensional analysis.

Additional velocity scales, rests, forces, cutoffs, or detector resolution introduce dimensionless ratios. These cannot be removed by the same choice of units. A physical comparison must report them.

## The gamma and beta functions

For positive real $z$,

$$
\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty u^{z-1}e^{-u}du.
$$

Integration by parts gives $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$, with $\Gamma(1)=1$, hence $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$. The Gaussian integral gives $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$. The recurrence extends the function to noninteger negative arguments, except at its poles. For $1<\gamma<2$, $\Gamma(1-\gamma)$ is negative because $\Gamma(2-\gamma)=(1-\gamma)\Gamma(1-\gamma)>0$. This sign is crucial in the stable-limit coefficient.

The beta integral is

$$
B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}du
=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)},\qquad a,b>0.
$$

To derive it, multiply the two gamma integrals and change variables from positive $x,y$ to $r=x+y$ and $u=x/(x+y)$. The Jacobian is $r$. The integral factors into $\Gamma(a+b)$ and $B(a,b)$. Substituting $w=u/(1-u)$ gives the alternative integral on $(0,\infty)$ used for duration moments.

## Survival, hazard, and conditional residual time

Given a duration with density $\psi$, its survival is $\Psi(a)=\Pr(\tau>a)$. Conditional on having reached age $a$, the probability of surviving another time $u$ is

$$
\Pr(\tau>a+u\mid\tau>a)=\frac{\Psi(a+u)}{\Psi(a)}.
$$

Its residual density is $\psi(a+u)/\Psi(a)$. The hazard $\lambda(a)=-d\log\Psi(a)/da$ follows by taking $u$ infinitesimal. Integrating gives $\Psi(a)=\exp[-\int_0^a\lambda(b)db]$.

For the Lomax family, conditional residual survival is $[1+u/(\tau_0+a)]^{-\gamma}$. It has the same functional family but an age-dependent scale $\tau_0+a$. This is a precise sense in which an old flight can be expected to keep going. If $\gamma\le1$, even its conditional residual mean is infinite. For $\gamma>1$, that mean is $(\tau_0+a)/(\gamma-1)$.

There are two distinct sampling experiments. Sampling a fresh duration uses $\psi$. Choosing a random time in a stationary renewal record preferentially selects long durations. The total selected interval has density $\ell\psi(\ell)/\mu$, and, conditional on its length $\ell$, the age is uniform on $(0,\ell)$. Integrating over $\ell$ yields the stationary age density $\Psi(a)/\mu$. This length-bias mechanism explains why initial conditions affect correlation functions even when the repeated duration law is unchanged.

## A practical Laplace asymptotic argument

Suppose $\Psi(t)\sim c t^{-\gamma}$ with $0<\gamma<1$. In its Laplace integral, set $u=st$:

$$
\widetilde\Psi(s)=s^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\Psi(u/s)du
\sim c s^{\gamma-1}\Gamma(1-\gamma).
$$

For small $s$, most of this singular contribution comes from large times of order $1/s$. The finite-time part contributes a bounded correction and is subleading to $s^{\gamma-1}$. The survival-transform identity then gives $1-\widetilde\psi(s)\sim c\Gamma(1-\gamma)s^\gamma$.

For $1<\gamma<2$ the integral of $\Psi$ is the finite mean $\mu$, so instead examine

$$
\mu-\widetilde\Psi(s)=\int_0^\infty(1-e^{-st})\Psi(t)dt
\sim c s^{\gamma-1}\int_0^\infty(1-e^{-u})u^{-\gamma}du.
$$

Integration by parts evaluates the last integral as $\Gamma(2-\gamma)/(\gamma-1)=-\Gamma(1-\gamma)$. Thus $\widetilde\psi(s)=1-\mu s-c\Gamma(1-\gamma)s^\gamma+o(s^\gamma)$, with a positive nonanalytic coefficient. These manipulations also explain why the cases $\gamma=1,2$ produce logarithms rather than ordinary powers.

The forward inference from a well-behaved positive tail to a small-$s$ singularity is an Abelian argument. The reverse inference generally needs regularity assumptions, such as the regular variation and positivity satisfied by the duration laws here. Arbitrary oscillatory functions can defeat a naive term-by-term inversion. Throughout the book asymptotic inversions are applied to these regular renewal distributions.

## A fractional material derivative

Advection at velocity $v$ is generated by $D_v=\partial_t+v\partial_x$. Its transform on a zero-history causal function has symbol $s-ikv$, with the initial term handled separately. For $0<\gamma<1$, define a Riemann–Liouville type material operator by

$$
D_v^\gamma f(x,t)=D_v\left[\frac1{\Gamma(1-\gamma)}
\int_0^t(t-u)^{-\gamma}f(x-v(t-u),u)du\right].
$$

The memory samples points on the characteristic ending at $(x,t)$, not at a fixed $x$. To check its symbol, transform the integral in space. The shift contributes $e^{ikv(t-u)}$. The Laplace convolution therefore has transform $(s-ikv)^{\gamma-1}\widetilde f(k,s)$. Acting with $D_v$ gives $(s-ikv)^\gamma\widetilde f$ when the causal boundary contribution is treated by this definition.

This operator couples memory and transport. Replacing it by $\partial_t^\gamma+v\partial_x^\gamma$ generally gives a different symbol and a different stochastic process. When deriving a fractional equation, specify both its transform symbol and its source or initial terms; naming an operator is not enough to determine a propagator.

## The velocity–MSD relation and stationarity

For any integrable velocity trajectory, $X(t)=\int_0^tV(u)du$. Squaring and averaging gives

$$
\langle X^2(t)\rangle=\int_0^tdu\int_0^tdw\,\langle V(u)V(w)\rangle.
$$

If the process is stationary with zero mean, the covariance depends only on the time difference, $C(|u-w|)$. The square then reduces to two triangles:

$$
\langle X^2(t)\rangle=2\int_0^t(t-u)C(u)du.
$$ {#eq-toolbox-green-kubo}

If $\int_0^\infty C(u)du$ is finite, the diffusion coefficient is that integral. If $C(u)\sim c u^{-\eta}$ with $0<\eta<1$, the weighted integral in @eq-toolbox-green-kubo instead gives $\langle X^2(t)\rangle\sim2c\,t^{2-\eta}/[(1-\eta)(2-\eta)]$. A fresh nonexponential renewal process is not stationary. Its correlation is $C(u,w)$, and substituting only the correlation from time zero into @eq-toolbox-green-kubo can give an incorrect prefactor or exponent. Chapter 5 develops the proper preparation-dependent correlations.

## Inferring a power law from a record

Suppose independent durations above a fixed lower threshold $\tau_{\min}$ follow the exact Pareto density $p(\tau)=\gamma\tau_{\min}^\gamma\tau^{-1-\gamma}$. Its log likelihood is

$$
\log L=n\log\gamma+n\gamma\log\tau_{\min}-(1+\gamma)\sum_{j=1}^n\log\tau_j.
$$

Differentiation gives $\widehat\gamma=n/\sum_j\log(\tau_j/\tau_{\min})$. This is a model-specific estimator, not a universal recipe. It assumes the threshold is fixed, observations are independent, and none are censored. If an observation ends while a flight is still running, the correct likelihood contribution is its survival $\Psi(a)$, not its completion density $\psi(a)$. A finite field of view can produce additional state-dependent truncation.

For an exact Pareto law, $\log(\tau/\tau_{\min})$ is exponential with rate $\gamma$, so the estimator's large-$n$ standard error is approximately $\gamma/\sqrt n$. Correlations reduce the effective sample size. A defensible analysis compares plausible alternatives, checks threshold sensitivity, simulates the observation procedure, and reports uncertainty. The data chapter explains why long-tailed displacements and long-tailed run times are different observables.

## A final integrative exercise

A particle has $v=2\,\mathrm{\mu m\,s^{-1}}$, $\tau_0=1\,\mathrm{s}$, and Lomax durations with $\gamma=3/2$. It is initialized at a renewal. Predict its asymptotic central scale, its MSD coefficient, and its maximum displacement at $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$. Explain which prediction is exact at that time.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked solution
The central stable length is $(K_{3/2}t)^{2/3}$ with $K_{3/2}=\sqrt{\pi/2}v^{3/2}\tau_0^{1/2}\simeq3.54\,\mathrm{\mu m^{3/2}\,s^{-1}}$. At $100\,\mathrm{s}$ the scale is about $50\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. The asymptotic MSD is $(4/3)v^2\sqrt{\tau_0}\,t^{3/2}\simeq5333\,\mathrm{\mu m^2}$, so its root is about $73\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. Neither number is an exact finite-time prediction; corrections can remain. The support bound $|X|\le vt=200\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ is exact for every realization. The stable scale is a shape parameter, not its root mean square, because the stable limiting law has an infinite second moment.
:::
